question: What is the primary function of the systemic circulation?

options.A: Transporting blood exclusively to the lungs
options.B: Supplying oxygenated blood to body organs
options.C: Producing red blood cells for circulation
options.D: Removing nutrients from active muscle tissues

explanation: Systemic circulation carries oxygen and essential nutrients from the left side of the heart out to the peripheral tissues and organs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is the vascular network described as a closed loop?

options.A: Blood circulates continuously through the heart and vessels without leaving the network
options.B: Capillaries possess solid walls that prevent any exchange of dissolved gases
options.C: Fluid enters the vascular system from tissues but never escapes back out
options.D: Valves permanently seal off the arteries from direct contact with body tissues

explanation: A closed loop means blood remains contained inside the heart and blood vessels during normal transport, rather than freely bathing organs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which blood vessels are primarily responsible for controlling resistance to blood flow?
explanation: Arterioles possess significant smooth muscle in their walls, allowing them to constrict or dilate to control vascular resistance and local pressure. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h2)

question: A patient has rigid, calcified large arteries. What direct mechanical consequence does this create?

options.A: Reduced ability to expand and dampen high pressure pulses
options.B: Immediate collapse of downstream capillary beds from zero pressure
options.C: Total reversal of blood flow back toward the heart
options.D: Massive pooling of blood within the superficial veins

explanation: Elastic arteries normally stretch to absorb the pressure wave generated by ventricular contraction, a property that is lost when walls become stiff. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h2)

question: What structural feature makes capillaries ideal for substance exchange?

options.A: Numerous internal valves that trap fluid in the tissues
options.B: Continuous smooth muscle contractions that pump fluids
options.C: Thick muscular layers that generate high internal pressure
options.D: Extremely thin walls made of a single cell layer

explanation: The single endothelial layer reduces the distance that oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nutrients must cross during diffusion. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h3)

question: Which body tissue would naturally contain the densest network of capillaries?
explanation: Active tissues like skeletal muscle require high amounts of oxygen and nutrient exchange, prompting a dense capillary supply compared to avascular structures. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of valves inside peripheral veins?

options.A: Accelerating blood speed through the capillary beds
options.B: Regulating the systemic arterial blood pressure
options.C: Filtering metabolic waste products out of plasma
options.D: Preventing the backward flow of blood against gravity

explanation: Venous valves act as one-way gates that ensure blood moves toward the heart rather than pooling downward in the extremities. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h4)

question: A patient remains bedridden for weeks. Why does this put them at high risk for venous stasis?

options.A: The heart pumps with excess force that damages vein valves
options.B: Capillary walls thicken and block fluid from entering venules
options.C: Absence of skeletal muscle contractions slows venous return
options.D: Arterial pressure drops so low that veins instantly collapse

explanation: Normal venous return relies heavily on the milking action of contracting skeletal muscles; immobility stops this pump, causing blood to pool. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which layer of a blood vessel wall is composed mainly of smooth muscle?
explanation: The middle layer, tunica media, contains smooth muscle cells and elastic tissue that manage vessel tone and caliber. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h5)

question: What would happen if the endothelial lining (tunica intima) of a blood vessel becomes damaged?

options.A: The tunica media dissolves due to exposure to plasma
options.B: Blood pressure in that specific vessel drops immediately to zero
options.C: Oxygen exchange in nearby capillaries stops permanently
options.D: Platelets may stick to the rough surface and form a clot

explanation: A smooth endothelium prevents inappropriate coagulation; damage exposes underlying collagen, triggering platelet adhesion and thrombus formation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h5)

question: What factor has the greatest immediate effect on changing vascular resistance?

options.B: Total volume of red blood cells
options.D: Total length of the vascular tree

explanation: Small changes in vessel radius produce exponential changes in resistance, making constriction and dilation powerful tools for blood pressure regulation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h6)

question: A patient experiences severe dehydration leading to increased blood viscosity. How does this affect blood flow?

options.A: Resistance decreases and blood moves much faster through vessels
options.B: Resistance increases and makes it harder for blood to circulate
options.C: Blood pressure drops to zero because fluid volume is low
options.D: Vessel radius expands instantly to compensate for thick blood

explanation: Higher viscosity means thicker blood creates more friction against vessel walls, increasing resistance and slowing down overall flow. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary pathological feature of atherosclerosis?

options.A: Complete destruction of all systemic capillaries
options.B: Excessive thickening of the tunica intima lining
options.C: Stretching and weakening of superficial vein valves
options.D: Fatty plaque buildup narrowing the arterial lumen

explanation: Atherosclerosis is characterized by lipid deposits and plaque accumulation inside arteries, which narrows the channel and restricts flow. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why is an untreated arterial aneurysm considered a medical emergency?

options.A: The weakened wall can rupture and cause life-threatening internal bleeding
options.B: It instantly thickens the blood and causes systemic clotting
options.C: The affected artery permanently closes off and creates new pathways
options.D: It automatically stops all blood flow to the lower extremities

explanation: An aneurysm is a localized dilation of a stressed, fragile arterial wall; if it bursts, catastrophic hemorrhage follows rapidly. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T5#GNS111_U2_T5_h7)
